title: Central torus radical and semisimple quotient of a reductive group
statement:
Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field] and let $G$ be a smooth [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms] affine group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism] over $k$, geometrically connected and reductive. Here geometrically connected means connected after extension to an algebraic closure, with connected as in [def-weil-connected-scheme]; reductive means that $G_{\bar k}$ has no nontrivial smooth connected normal unipotent closed subgroup scheme, for an algebraic closure $\bar k$ of $k$. Closed normal subgroups are as in [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. For smooth affine groups, unipotent means that in a faithful matrix representation every geometric point is a unipotent matrix, that is, $(u-I)^N=0$ for some $N\geq1$.

The group $G$ has a largest smooth connected normal solvable closed subgroup scheme $R(G)$, called its radical. Solvable means having a finite descending series of closed subgroup schemes, each normal in its predecessor, in which every successive group-scheme quotient is commutative. The centre $Z(G)$ is the subgroup functor whose $A$-points are the elements of $G(A)$ commuting with every element of $G(A')$ for every commutative $A$-algebra $A'$. Then $R(G)$ is the largest subtorus of $Z(G)$. A torus is a group scheme which after extension to $\bar k$ is isomorphic to $(\mathbf G_m)^d$ for some $d\geq0$, with $\mathbf G_m$ as in [def-sc-gm-ga]. Moreover $R(G)_{\bar k}=R(G_{\bar k})$, and the fppf sheaf quotient $Q=G/R(G)$ is represented by a smooth affine geometrically connected group scheme of finite type over $k$ which is semisimple and reductive. Here semisimple means that $Q_{\bar k}$ has no nontrivial smooth connected normal solvable closed subgroup scheme; in particular $Q_{\bar k}$ has no nontrivial smooth connected normal unipotent closed subgroup scheme. The fppf sheaf quotient is the sheafification of $A\mapsto G(A)/R(G)(A)$ for faithfully flat finitely presented coverings of commutative $k$-algebras.

source.place: Corollary 17.62(b)--(d), printed pp.372--373; Sections 6.44--6.46, printed p.135, and Chapter 19(a)--(b), printed pp.397--400. The quotient is by the smooth central torus, with the usual algebraic-group quotient of Theorem 5.28 and Propositions 5.24--5.29 (torsor, smoothness and affineness).

proof.text: Among the smooth connected normal solvable closed subgroups of $G$, choose $R$ of greatest dimension; this is possible since the trivial subgroup is one and the dimensions are nonnegative integers bounded by $\dim G$. For any other such subgroup $N$, [lem-sfb-solvable-normal-subgroup-products] gives another such subgroup $RN$ containing $R$ and $N$. Maximality of the dimension and strict dimension growth for a proper closed inclusion force $RN=R$, hence $N\subseteq R$. This proves existence and uniqueness of $R=R(G)$. The same argument constructs $C=R(G_{\bar k})$.

source.place: Lemma 6.41, Proposition 6.42 and Section 6.44, printed pp.134--135.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-perfect-solvable-unipotent-torus] over the perfect field $\bar k$ to $C$. Its smooth connected unipotent subgroup $C_u$ is normal in $G_{\bar k}$ because $C$ is normal there and the ambient group is smooth. Reductivity of $G$ forces $C_u=1$, so $C=C/C_u$ is a torus. By the field-extension assertion of [lem-sfb-solvable-normal-subgroup-products], $R_{\bar k}$ is a smooth connected normal solvable subgroup of $G_{\bar k}$; thus $R_{\bar k}\subseteq C$. The smooth connected subgroup assertion of [lem-sfb-multiplicative-type-largest-subtorus] makes $R_{\bar k}$ a torus, so it is a product of copies of $\mathbf G_m$ over $\bar k$. This is exactly the stated definition that $R$ is a $k$-torus.

source.place: Corollary 17.62(b), printed p.372; Theorem 16.33(a)--(c) and Proposition 1.90.

proof.text: Normality gives a conjugation action $G\times R\to R$ by group automorphisms. Since $G$ is smooth and geometrically connected and $R$ is a torus, [lem-sfb-connected-action-torus-rigidity] makes this action the projection: $grg^{-1}=r$ after every change of scalar algebra. Hence $R\subseteq Z(G)$ for precisely the centre functor in the statement.

The functor $Z(G)$ is a closed normal commutative subgroup by [lem-sfb-affine-group-centre-base-change]. It is of multiplicative type by [lem-sfb-reductive-centre-multiplicative-type], so [lem-sfb-multiplicative-type-largest-subtorus] supplies its largest subtorus $T=Z(G)^t$. This $T$ is smooth and connected, since every torus is by the same [lem-sfb-multiplicative-type-largest-subtorus], is normal in $G$ since it is central, and is solvable: the series $T\supseteq1$ has commutative quotient $T$. Thus maximality of $R$ gives $T\subseteq R$. Conversely Step 3 makes $R$ a subtorus of $Z(G)$, so $R\subseteq T$. Therefore $R=Z(G)^t$.

source.place: Corollary 17.62(a)--(b), printed p.372; Notation 12.29, printed p.241.

proof.text: Applying the argument of Steps 1--4 to $G_{\bar k}$ gives $C=Z(G_{\bar k})^t$; all the hypotheses hold there by the geometric reductivity assumption. Using separately base change for the scheme-theoretic centre and for the largest subtorus gives the equality of closed subgroups $$R_{\bar k}=(Z(G)^t)_{\bar k}=(Z(G)_{\bar k})^t=Z(G_{\bar k})^t=C.$$ Thus $R(G)_{\bar k}=R(G_{\bar k})$, without asserting such a base-change theorem for the radicals of arbitrary nonreductive groups.

Apply [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry] to the closed normal subgroup $R\subseteq G$. It represents exactly the fppf sheaf quotient specified in the statement by an affine finite-type group $Q$, which is smooth and geometrically connected since $G$ is. The same cited statement identifies $$Q_{\bar k}\simeq G_{\bar k}/R_{\bar k}=G_{\bar k}/C$$ compatibly with the quotient map and its kernel, using Step 5.

source.place: Propositions 5.24--5.29, printed pp.104--105; Corollary 17.62(d), printed p.373.

proof.text: Let $S\subseteq Q_{\bar k}$ be any smooth connected normal solvable closed subgroup and let $P$ be its inverse image in $G_{\bar k}$. The exact-sequence and subgroup-correspondence assertions of [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry] give $1\to C\to P\to S\to1$, with $P$ smooth and connected and normal in $G_{\bar k}$. Pull back a solvable series for $S$; the successive quotients above $C$ are the original commutative quotients, by that correspondence assertion. Append a solvable series for $C$. This is a finite solvable series for $P$. Consequently $P\subseteq C$ by the maximality proved in Step 1, while the inverse image contains $C$; hence $P=C$ and exactness forces $S=P/C=1$. This proves the geometric semisimplicity required. Finally [lem-sfb-smooth-unipotent-solvable] makes every smooth connected normal unipotent subgroup of $Q_{\bar k}$ solvable, so the same conclusion makes it trivial. Together with Step 6 this proves that $Q$ is reductive as well.

source.place: Section 6.44, printed p.135; Proposition 19.2(b), printed p.398; Corollary 17.62(d), printed p.373; Theorem 14.5 and Example 6.49.

proof_origin.place: Corollary 17.62(b)--(d), printed pp.372--373, expanding radical existence by Lemma 6.41/Proposition 6.42 and quotient semisimplicity by the inverse-image argument of Proposition 19.2(b), printed p.398.
